Roofman is a gem of a crowdpleaser from Derek Cianfrance and Channing Tatum.

“Roofman” might not seem like it’s tied to Cianfrance's usual formula given how funny it is, but stick with it long enough and you’ll find yourself in the midst of another couple headed for a heartbreaking finale.

It works mostly because of Tatum and Dunst, a rare on-screen pairing of single parents in their 40s, both trying to navigate a stressful situation, hard enough even without the criminality. There’s real chemistry there.
In a vacuum, there’s a lot about Roofman that exudes a degree of charm, namely Tatum’s performance as Manchester.
A career-best performance by Channing Tatum. The kind of movie they don't make enough of anymore.
Tatum basically oozes charisma, and you’re reminded of what a better actor he actually is than most Academy Award-winning A-listers.

As a rare true-crime drama that doesn’t just replay its wild supermarket headline but finds the soul beating underneath it, Cianfrance turns Roofman’s unbelievable premise into something refreshingly sweet and human.

The tonal juggling act isn’t always seamless, but in a way, the contradictions are what give “Roofman” its life. It’s a sad movie, really, but it’s also a lot of fun. And if that doesn’t make sense, maybe it’s the whole point.

Unfortunately, however, “Roofman” also capitulates to the feel-good demands of Hollywood storytelling, leaving the pricklier aspects of Manchester’s story on the table. And the film is forgettable as a result.
In the end, it’s the through-the-roof chemistry between the two leads that makes the film worthy of repeat viewing.
Cinefrance keeps it real despite the crazy nature of what actually happened and makes one of those studio movies that studios just don’t seem interested in making much anymore. This time they did.
